(i) the amino-terminal residues of a peptide are the most important for binding to MHC molecules and (ii) the amino-terminal residue of a peptide must be hydrophilic in order for the peptide to bind MHC class II.

the major histocompatibility class II molecule of mice, IAd, interacts with peptides that contain a sequence motif consisting of a central hydrophobic amino acid flanked by hydrophilic residues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of structural requirements for the binding of peptides to MHC molecules, and the development of procedures to predict such binding.
the identification of the molecular basis of antigenic determinants.
the identification of structural features which are necessary and sufficient to confer antigenicity on peptide molecules.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the two procedures described in this report can be successfully applied to predict the capacity of peptides to bind IAd and I Ed molecules, and that they are therefore useful tools for the identification of potential immunogenic peptide regions in proteins.
the two procedures we describe here, which are based on the analysis of amino acid sequence patterns, are of great value for predicting peptide-MHC interactions.

the two procedures described here, although not infallible, are very efficient and should be useful in the prediction of the binding capacity of peptides to MHC class II proteins of the d haploid type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the case of MHC class II binding peptides, the sequence motifs that are predictive for binding can be defined by simple amino acid composition.
the IAd and IAd molecules have similar but not identical binding motifs.
a peptide is likely to be an MHC ligand if it contains a stretch of at least nine amino acid residues that is rich in hydrophobic, acidic, and/or basic residues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not the amino acid sequence of a peptide that determines the interaction with the MHC, but the structural characteristics that are conferred on the peptide by its amino acid sequence.
the MHC binding motif is a sequence pattern that can be used to predict the capacity of peptides to bind to the I-A d molecules.
the MHC binding motifs are not only a tool to predict the binding of a given peptide, but can also be used to identify the immunogenicity of a protein.
